2 Chronicles 1.summary: Solomon is established as king, and he takes all Israel's leaders to the high place at Gibeon, where Moses' tabernacle and the brasen altar still stand (2 Chronicles 1:1–5). He offers a thousand burnt offerings there (2 Chronicles 1:6). That night God tells him to ask for anything, and Solomon asks, "Give me now wisdom and knowledge" to lead the people (2 Chronicles 1:7–10). God grants it and adds riches, wealth, and honor beyond any king before or after him (2 Chronicles 1:11–12). Solomon gathers chariots and horsemen and makes silver and gold as common as stones in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 1:13–17).
2 Chronicles 1.whereWeAre: 1 Chronicles ended with David's death and Solomon on the throne. Now Solomon goes to the tabernacle at Gibeon, asks God for wisdom, and receives riches and honor too. In chapter 2 he begins preparing to build the temple.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Worships at Gibeon and asks God for wisdom to judge his people.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Appears to Solomon at night and gives him wisdom, riches, and honor.

keyThemes.explanation: Offered anything, Solomon asks for wisdom to lead God's people, not for riches or long life.
Because Solomon asked rightly, God adds riches and honor to the wisdom.
Solomon's reign begins with sacrifices at the tabernacle before any building starts.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Solomon asking God for wisdom at Gibeon.

2 Chronicles 2.summary: Solomon decides to build a house for the name of the LORD and a palace, and he sets thousands of men to carry loads and cut stone (2 Chronicles 2:1–2). He asks Huram king of Tyre for cedar and a skilled worker, saying that "the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain him" (2 Chronicles 2:3–10). Huram blesses the LORD and sends a master craftsman, also named Huram, whose mother was from the tribe of Dan (2 Chronicles 2:11–14). Huram promises to float timber to Joppa in return for wheat, barley, wine, and oil (2 Chronicles 2:15–16). Solomon counts the strangers living in Israel and puts them to work on the building (2 Chronicles 2:17–18).
2 Chronicles 2.whereWeAre: God gave Solomon wisdom and wealth in chapter 1. Now Solomon gathers workers and asks Huram king of Tyre for cedar and a master craftsman. Chapter 3 begins the building on mount Moriah.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Plans the temple and asks Tyre for timber and a craftsman.

keyFigures.name: Huram king of Tyre
keyFigures.role: Blesses the LORD and sends cedar and a skilled worker.

keyFigures.name: Huram the craftsman
keyFigures.role: A master worker, son of a woman of Dan, sent to lead the skilled work.

keyThemes.theme: A house too small for God
keyThemes.explanation: Solomon builds a great house, yet admits no building can contain the God of heaven.
A foreign king praises the LORD and supplies wood and skill for the temple.
Solomon plans workers, materials, and payment before the building begins.

2 Chronicles 3.summary: Solomon begins building the house of the LORD on mount Moriah, at the threshingfloor of Ornan, where the LORD had appeared to David (2 Chronicles 3:1–2). The porch and the great house are lined with gold and decorated with precious stones and carved cherubims (2 Chronicles 3:3–7). The most holy house is overlaid with fine gold, and two large cherubims stand in it with wings touching wall to wall (2 Chronicles 3:8–13). Solomon makes the vail of blue, purple, and crimson, and sets up two bronze pillars named Jachin and Boaz before the temple (2 Chronicles 3:14–17).
2 Chronicles 3.whereWeAre: Solomon arranged for workers and timber in chapter 2. Now the temple rises on mount Moriah, with gold walls, carved cherubims, and two bronze pillars. Chapter 4 describes the furnishings made for it.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Builds the house of the LORD on mount Moriah.

keyThemes.explanation: The temple stands where God appeared to David, on mount Moriah.
Gold, precious stones, and carved cherubims show the honor due to God's house.
The most holy place and the vail mark the place where God meets his people.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Solomon building the temple, with different selections of details.

2 Chronicles 4.summary: Solomon makes a bronze altar twenty cubits square and a great molten sea resting on twelve bronze oxen (2 Chronicles 4:1–5). He makes ten lavers for washing, ten golden candlesticks, ten tables, and a hundred gold basons (2 Chronicles 4:6–8). He builds the court of the priests and the great court (2 Chronicles 4:9–10). Huram finishes the bronze work, cast in clay in the plain of Jordan, in such amounts that its weight could not be found out (2 Chronicles 4:11–18). The altar of gold, the lampstands, and the other vessels inside the house are made of pure gold (2 Chronicles 4:19–22).
2 Chronicles 4.whereWeAre: The temple building was finished in chapter 3. This chapter lists what was made for its worship: the bronze altar, the great molten sea, lavers, lampstands, tables, and gold vessels. In chapter 5 the ark is brought in.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Has the altar, the molten sea, and the gold vessels made.

keyFigures.name: Huram
keyFigures.role: The craftsman who finishes the bronze work for the temple.

keyThemes.explanation: The great bronze altar is ready for the burnt offerings.
The molten sea and the lavers are for washing the priests and the offerings.
The golden lampstands and tables carry on the work of the tabernacle on a larger scale.

2 Chronicles 5.summary: Solomon brings David's dedicated treasures into the finished house (2 Chronicles 5:1). At the feast of the seventh month, the elders gather, the Levites take up the ark, and Solomon and the people sacrifice more sheep and oxen than can be counted (2 Chronicles 5:2–6). The priests set the ark in the most holy place under the cherubims' wings, and nothing is in it but the two tables of stone (2 Chronicles 5:7–10). As the singers and trumpeters praise the LORD "as one," a cloud fills the house, and the priests cannot stand to minister (2 Chronicles 5:11–14).
2 Chronicles 5.whereWeAre: The temple and its furnishings were finished in chapters 3–4. Now the priests carry the ark into the most holy place, the singers praise God, and a cloud fills the house. In chapter 6 Solomon prays at the dedication.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Gathers Israel and brings the ark into the temple.

keyFigures.name: The priests
keyFigures.role: Set the ark in the most holy place and blow the trumpets.

keyFigures.name: The Levite singers
keyFigures.role: Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun's men, who praise the LORD as the cloud fills the house.

keyThemes.explanation: The cloud of glory fills the temple as it once filled the tabernacle.
Singers and trumpeters join "as one" to praise God's goodness and mercy.
The ark holds the tables of stone, the covenant God made at Horeb.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: The ark entering the completed temple and God's glory filling it.

2 Chronicles 6.summary: Solomon blesses the people and tells how God kept his promise to David by choosing Jerusalem and letting David's son build the house (2 Chronicles 6:1–11). Kneeling on a bronze scaffold before all Israel, he praises God for keeping covenant and asks, "will God in very deed dwell with men on the earth?" (2 Chronicles 6:12–21). He asks God to hear prayers made toward this house in times of sin, defeat, drought, famine, and plague (2 Chronicles 6:22–31). He prays for the stranger who comes from a far country, for armies at war, and for captives who repent in a foreign land (2 Chronicles 6:32–39). He ends by asking God to arise into his resting place and to remember his mercies to David (2 Chronicles 6:40–42).
2 Chronicles 6.whereWeAre: The cloud of the LORD's glory filled the temple in chapter 5. Now Solomon blesses the people and prays that God will hear every prayer made toward this house. Chapter 7 tells how God answers, with fire from heaven.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Blesses the people and prays at the dedication of the temple.

keyThemes.explanation: Solomon's prayer begins by praising God for keeping his word to David.
Solomon asks God to hear every prayer made toward this house.
Again and again Solomon asks God to forgive when his people turn back to him.
Solomon also asks God to hear foreigners who come to pray, so all may know his name.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Solomon's prayer at the temple dedication.

2 Chronicles 7.summary: When Solomon finishes praying, fire comes down from heaven and consumes the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD fills the house (2 Chronicles 7:1–3). Solomon and the people offer 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep and keep the dedication and the feast for fourteen days (2 Chronicles 7:4–11). The LORD appears to Solomon by night and promises, "If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray... then will I hear from heaven" (2 Chronicles 7:12–18). He warns that if they turn away to other gods, he will pluck them out of the land and make the temple a byword among the nations (2 Chronicles 7:19–22).
2 Chronicles 7.whereWeAre: Solomon finished his dedication prayer in chapter 6. Now fire falls from heaven, the people celebrate for two weeks, and God appears to Solomon at night with a promise and a warning. Chapter 8 turns to the rest of Solomon's work.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Finishes the dedication and keeps the feast with all Israel.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Sends fire from heaven and appears to Solomon with a promise and a warning.

keyFigures.name: The people of Israel
keyFigures.role: Bow on the pavement and praise, "For he is good."

keyThemes.explanation: Fire from heaven shows that God accepts the temple and its sacrifices.
God promises to forgive and heal the land when his people humble themselves and turn.
If Israel turns to other gods, even this great temple will be cast off.

2 Chronicles 8.summary: After twenty years of building, Solomon builds cities, store cities, and fortresses, including Tadmor in the wilderness and both Bethhorons (2 Chronicles 8:1–6). He makes the peoples left from the Canaanites his forced laborers, while Israelites serve as soldiers and officers (2 Chronicles 8:7–10). He moves Pharaoh's daughter out of the city of David because the places where the ark had been are holy (2 Chronicles 8:11). He keeps the daily, sabbath, new moon, and feast offerings and sets the priests and Levites in their courses as David commanded (2 Chronicles 8:12–16). Huram's sailors take Solomon's ships from Eziongeber to Ophir and bring back 450 talents of gold (2 Chronicles 8:17–18).
2 Chronicles 8.whereWeAre: God answered Solomon's prayer in chapter 7. Now Solomon builds cities, sets up the daily worship David planned, and sends ships to Ophir for gold. In chapter 9 the queen of Sheba comes to see his wisdom.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Builds cities, orders the temple worship, and sends ships to Ophir.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh's daughter
keyFigures.role: Solomon's wife, moved to a house away from the city of David.

keyFigures.name: Huram
keyFigures.role: King of Tyre, who sends ships and skilled sailors.

keyThemes.explanation: Solomon keeps the offerings and courses of priests and Levites as Moses and David commanded.
Solomon moves Pharaoh's daughter out because the places where the ark had been are holy.
Building, labor, and trade show how strong Solomon's kingdom has become.

2 Chronicles 9.summary: The queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with hard questions, and he answers them all (2 Chronicles 9:1–2). She tells him "the one half of the greatness of thy wisdom was not told me" and praises the LORD, and the two exchange rich gifts (2 Chronicles 9:3–12). Solomon's yearly gold, his gold shields, his ivory throne, and his ships of Tarshish make him greater than all the kings of the earth (2 Chronicles 9:13–28). He reigns forty years over all Israel, dies, and his son Rehoboam becomes king (2 Chronicles 9:29–31).
2 Chronicles 9.whereWeAre: Chapter 8 showed Solomon's building and trade. Now the queen of Sheba visits, and the chapter describes his great wealth before his death after forty years. In chapter 10 his son Rehoboam loses most of the kingdom.

keyFigures.name: The queen of Sheba
keyFigures.role: Tests Solomon with hard questions and praises his God.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Answers her questions and rules with great wealth for forty years.

keyFigures.name: Rehoboam
keyFigures.role: Solomon's son, who becomes king when he dies.

keyThemes.explanation: The queen of Sheba sees Solomon's wisdom and praises the God who made him king.
Solomon's great riches fulfill God's promise at Gibeon.
After forty years Solomon dies, and the kingdom passes to his son.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: The queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon.

2 Chronicles 10.summary: Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be made king, and Jeroboam comes back from Egypt to lead the people's request for a lighter load (2 Chronicles 10:1–5). Rehoboam rejects the advice of the old men and follows the young men, answering, "my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions" (2 Chronicles 10:6–14). The writer says "the cause was of God," to fulfill his word through Ahijah (2 Chronicles 10:15). Israel cries, "To your tents, O Israel," stones Hadoram the tax master, and rebels against the house of David (2 Chronicles 10:16–19).
2 Chronicles 10.whereWeAre: Solomon died at the end of chapter 9. Now Rehoboam refuses to lighten the people's load, and the northern tribes break away under Jeroboam. From chapter 11 on, Chronicles follows only the kings of Judah.

keyFigures.name: Rehoboam
keyFigures.role: Rejects the old men's advice and loses the northern tribes.

keyFigures.name: Jeroboam
keyFigures.role: Returns from Egypt and speaks for the people at Shechem.

keyFigures.name: The old men
keyFigures.role: Solomon's advisers, who tell Rehoboam to speak kindly.

keyFigures.name: The young men
keyFigures.role: Rehoboam's friends, who tell him to answer harshly.

keyFigures.name: Hadoram
keyFigures.role: Over the forced labor; Israel stones him.

keyThemes.explanation: Rehoboam rejects the wise counsel of the old men and loses most of his kingdom.
His hard answer to the people's request turns them against David's house.
The writer says the split came from God, as Ahijah had foretold.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Rehoboam's refusal and the division of the kingdom.

2 Chronicles 11.summary: Rehoboam gathers 180,000 men to win back Israel, but the prophet Shemaiah brings God's word, "Ye shall not go up, nor fight against your brethren," and they obey (2 Chronicles 11:1–4). Rehoboam builds fifteen fortified cities in Judah and Benjamin and stocks them with food and weapons (2 Chronicles 11:5–12). When Jeroboam casts out the LORD's priests, the priests and Levites move to Judah, along with others who seek the LORD, and they strengthen the kingdom for three years (2 Chronicles 11:13–17). Rehoboam takes many wives, loves Maachah the daughter of Absalom most, and makes her son Abijah chief among his sons (2 Chronicles 11:18–23).
2 Chronicles 11.whereWeAre: The northern tribes rejected Rehoboam in chapter 10. Now a prophet stops him from going to war, and he fortifies Judah while faithful priests and Levites move south. In chapter 12 Rehoboam forsakes the law, and Egypt invades.

keyFigures.name: Rehoboam
keyFigures.role: Obeys the word not to fight and fortifies Judah.

keyFigures.name: Shemaiah
keyFigures.role: A man of God who tells Rehoboam not to fight his brothers.

keyFigures.name: Jeroboam
keyFigures.role: Casts out the priests of the LORD and makes his own.

keyFigures.name: The priests and Levites
keyFigures.role: Leave their homes in the north and come to Judah.

keyFigures.name: Abijah
keyFigures.role: Son of Maachah, whom Rehoboam makes chief among his sons.

keyThemes.explanation: Rehoboam turns back from war when God's prophet tells him to.
Priests, Levites, and all who seek the LORD leave the north to worship in Jerusalem.
Judah is strong as long as it walks in the way of David and Solomon.

2 Chronicles 12.summary: Once Rehoboam's kingdom is strong, he and all Israel forsake the law of the LORD (2 Chronicles 12:1). In his fifth year Shishak king of Egypt invades with a huge army and takes Judah's fortified cities (2 Chronicles 12:2–4). Shemaiah tells the leaders that God has left them to Shishak, and when they humble themselves, God promises not to destroy them but to make them Shishak's servants (2 Chronicles 12:5–8). Shishak takes the treasures of the temple and palace, including Solomon's gold shields, and Rehoboam replaces them with bronze (2 Chronicles 12:9–12). Rehoboam reigns seventeen years and does evil "because he prepared not his heart to seek the LORD" (2 Chronicles 12:13–16).
2 Chronicles 12.whereWeAre: Chapter 11 showed Judah growing strong under Rehoboam. Once he is secure he forsakes the law, and Shishak of Egypt invades, but Judah is spared when its leaders humble themselves. In chapter 13 Rehoboam's son Abijah faces Jeroboam in battle.

keyFigures.name: Rehoboam
keyFigures.role: Forsakes the law, then humbles himself when Egypt invades.

keyFigures.name: Shishak
keyFigures.role: King of Egypt, who invades Judah and takes the temple treasures.

keyFigures.name: Shemaiah
keyFigures.role: The prophet who tells Judah's leaders that God has left them to Shishak.

keyFigures.name: The princes of Israel
keyFigures.role: Humble themselves and say, "The LORD is righteous."

keyThemes.explanation: When Rehoboam feels secure, he and Israel turn away from the LORD.
When the leaders humble themselves, God does not destroy them.
Judah serves Shishak so it will know the difference between serving God and serving foreign kings.

2 Chronicles 13.summary: Abijah becomes king and sets 400,000 men in battle against Jeroboam's 800,000 (2 Chronicles 13:1–3). From mount Zemaraim he reminds Israel of God's covenant with David and contrasts Judah's true priests with Jeroboam's golden calves, warning, "fight ye not against the LORD God of your fathers" (2 Chronicles 13:4–12). Jeroboam surrounds Judah with an ambush, but Judah cries to the LORD, the priests blow the trumpets, and God strikes Israel's army (2 Chronicles 13:13–17). Judah wins "because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers," and Jeroboam never recovers his strength (2 Chronicles 13:18–22).
2 Chronicles 13.whereWeAre: Rehoboam died at the end of chapter 12. Now his son Abijah faces Jeroboam's much larger army and wins because Judah relied on the LORD. In chapter 14 Abijah's son Asa begins his long reign.

keyFigures.name: Abijah
keyFigures.role: King of Judah, who calls Israel back to the LORD and wins the battle.

keyFigures.name: Jeroboam
keyFigures.role: King of Israel, whose larger army and ambush are defeated.

keyFigures.name: The priests
keyFigures.role: Blow the trumpets as Judah cries to the LORD.

keyThemes.explanation: Abijah reminds Israel that God gave the kingdom to David's line by "a covenant of salt."
Abijah contrasts Judah's priests and daily offerings with Jeroboam's golden calves.
Judah is outnumbered and surrounded but wins because it relies on the LORD.

2 Chronicles 14.summary: Abijah dies, and the land has ten years of quiet under his son Asa (2 Chronicles 14:1). Asa removes foreign altars and images, commands Judah to seek the LORD, and builds fortified cities (2 Chronicles 14:2–8). Zerah the Ethiopian comes against him with a huge army, and Asa prays, "help us, O LORD our God; for we rest on thee" (2 Chronicles 14:9–11). The LORD strikes the Ethiopians, and Judah chases them to Gerar and carries away much spoil (2 Chronicles 14:12–15).
2 Chronicles 14.whereWeAre: Abijah defeated Jeroboam in chapter 13. Now his son Asa removes idols, builds up Judah, and prays when a huge Ethiopian army attacks. In chapter 15 a prophet urges him to keep seeking God.

keyFigures.name: Asa
keyFigures.role: Removes idols, builds up Judah, and prays for help against Zerah.

keyFigures.name: Zerah the Ethiopian
keyFigures.role: Attacks Judah with a huge army and is routed.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Strikes the Ethiopians before Asa and Judah.

keyThemes.explanation: Asa removes idols, and God gives Judah years of quiet.
Facing a huge army, Asa prays that it is nothing for God to help the weak.
God strikes the Ethiopians, and Judah only gathers the spoil.

2 Chronicles 15.summary: The Spirit of God comes on Azariah the son of Oded, who tells Asa, "The LORD is with you, while ye be with him" (2 Chronicles 15:1–7). Asa takes courage, puts away the idols, and repairs the altar of the LORD, and many from the northern tribes come over to him (2 Chronicles 15:8–9). In his fifteenth year the people gather at Jerusalem, sacrifice, and swear with shouting and trumpets to seek the LORD with all their heart (2 Chronicles 15:10–15). Asa removes Maachah from being queen because of her idol, though the high places are not taken out of Israel (2 Chronicles 15:16–19).
2 Chronicles 15.whereWeAre: Asa won a great victory over Zerah in chapter 14. Now the prophet Azariah tells him, "if ye seek him, he will be found of you" (2 Chronicles 15:2), and Asa leads Judah in a covenant to seek the LORD. Chapter 16 shows Asa's last years, when he trusts in a foreign king instead.

keyFigures.name: Azariah son of Oded
keyFigures.role: A prophet who urges Asa to seek the LORD.

keyFigures.name: Asa
keyFigures.role: Puts away idols, leads a covenant, and removes his mother from being queen.

keyFigures.name: The people of Judah and Benjamin
keyFigures.role: Swear an oath to seek the LORD with all their heart.

keyFigures.name: Maachah
keyFigures.role: The queen mother, removed because she made an idol.

keyThemes.theme: God is found by those who seek
keyThemes.explanation: Azariah promises that God will be with them while they are with him.
The people swear with all their heart to seek the LORD.
Asa removes his own mother from being queen because of her idol.

2 Chronicles 16.summary: When Baasha king of Israel builds up Ramah against Judah, Asa sends silver and gold from the temple to Benhadad king of Syria to turn him against Israel (2 Chronicles 16:1–6). Hanani the seer tells Asa he has done foolishly by relying on Syria, for "the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth" (2 Chronicles 16:7–9). Asa puts Hanani in prison and oppresses some of the people (2 Chronicles 16:10). In his thirty-ninth year Asa's feet become badly diseased, yet he seeks the physicians and not the LORD, and he dies two years later (2 Chronicles 16:11–14).
2 Chronicles 16.whereWeAre: Asa led Judah in covenant renewal in chapter 15. Now, when Israel threatens him, he pays the king of Syria for help and jails the prophet who rebukes him. Chapter 17 begins the reign of his son Jehoshaphat.

keyFigures.name: Asa
keyFigures.role: Pays Syria for help, then jails the seer who rebukes him.

keyFigures.name: Baasha
keyFigures.role: King of Israel, who builds Ramah to cut off Judah.

keyFigures.name: Benhadad
keyFigures.role: King of Syria, who breaks his treaty with Israel for Asa's silver.

keyFigures.name: Hanani
keyFigures.role: The seer who rebukes Asa and is put in prison.

keyThemes.explanation: Asa pays a foreign king instead of relying on the LORD who saved him before.
Hanani says God's eyes search the earth to show himself strong for those whose hearts are true.

keyThemes.theme: A hard heart in old age
keyThemes.explanation: Asa jails the prophet and seeks only physicians in his illness.

2 Chronicles 17.summary: Jehoshaphat becomes king and strengthens Judah, and the LORD is with him because he walks in the first ways of David and does not seek Baalim (2 Chronicles 17:1–6). In his third year he sends princes, Levites, and priests to teach in all the cities of Judah, carrying "the book of the law of the LORD" with them (2 Chronicles 17:7–9). The fear of the LORD falls on the nearby kingdoms, so they make no war, and the Philistines and Arabians bring him gifts (2 Chronicles 17:10–11). Jehoshaphat grows great, building castles and store cities and keeping a large army (2 Chronicles 17:12–19).
2 Chronicles 17.whereWeAre: Asa ended his reign badly in chapter 16. His son Jehoshaphat seeks God, sends teachers of the law through Judah, and grows strong. In chapter 18 he makes a dangerous alliance with Ahab king of Israel.

keyFigures.name: Jehoshaphat
keyFigures.role: Seeks God, strengthens Judah, and sends teachers of the law.

keyFigures.name: The teachers of the law
keyFigures.role: Princes, Levites, and priests who teach in all the cities of Judah.

keyFigures.name: The Philistines and Arabians
keyFigures.role: Bring Jehoshaphat silver and flocks as gifts.

keyThemes.explanation: Jehoshaphat walks in David's first ways and seeks God rather than Baal.
Jehoshaphat sends teachers with the book of the law to every city.
The fear of the LORD keeps the nations around Judah from war.

2 Chronicles 18.summary: Jehoshaphat makes a marriage alliance with Ahab, and Ahab asks him to go to war at Ramothgilead (2 Chronicles 18:1–3). Four hundred prophets promise victory, but Jehoshaphat asks for a prophet of the LORD, and Micaiah is brought in (2 Chronicles 18:4–11). Micaiah says, "what my God saith, that will I speak," and tells of Israel scattered like sheep and a lying spirit in the prophets' mouths (2 Chronicles 18:12–22). Zedekiah strikes Micaiah, and Ahab has him put in prison until he returns (2 Chronicles 18:23–27). In battle Ahab disguises himself, Jehoshaphat cries out and God helps him, and an arrow shot at random kills Ahab at sunset (2 Chronicles 18:28–34).
2 Chronicles 18.whereWeAre: Jehoshaphat grew rich and strong in chapter 17. Now he joins Ahab in war at Ramothgilead, though the prophet Micaiah warns that Ahab will die. Chapter 19 shows a prophet rebuking Jehoshaphat for the alliance.

keyFigures.name: Jehoshaphat
keyFigures.role: Joins Ahab in battle but asks to hear a prophet of the LORD.

keyFigures.name: Ahab
keyFigures.role: King of Israel, who jails Micaiah and dies in battle in disguise.

keyFigures.name: Micaiah
keyFigures.role: A prophet who speaks only what God says and foretells Ahab's death.

keyFigures.name: Zedekiah son of Chenaanah
keyFigures.role: A prophet who makes horns of iron and strikes Micaiah.

keyFigures.name: The king of Syria
keyFigures.role: Orders his captains to fight only against the king of Israel.

keyThemes.explanation: Jehoshaphat's tie to Ahab nearly costs him his life.
Micaiah refuses to say what the king wants and speaks only what God says.
Ahab's disguise cannot save him from the arrow God's word foretold.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: The campaign at Ramoth-gilead and Ahab's death.

2 Chronicles 19.summary: When Jehoshaphat returns to Jerusalem, Jehu the son of Hanani asks him, "Shouldest thou help the ungodly," but also says good things are found in him (2 Chronicles 19:1–3). Jehoshaphat goes out among the people to bring them back to the LORD and sets judges in the fortified cities (2 Chronicles 19:4–5). He tells the judges, "ye judge not for man, but for the LORD," for with God there is no taking of gifts (2 Chronicles 19:6–7). In Jerusalem he appoints Levites, priests, and family heads to judge, with Amariah over the LORD's matters and Zebadiah over the king's (2 Chronicles 19:8–11).
2 Chronicles 19.whereWeAre: Jehoshaphat barely escaped the battle where Ahab died in chapter 18. Now the seer Jehu rebukes him, and Jehoshaphat appoints judges and tells them to judge in the fear of the LORD. In chapter 20 a great army comes against Judah.

keyFigures.name: Jehoshaphat
keyFigures.role: Hears the rebuke, turns the people back to God, and sets up judges.

keyFigures.name: Jehu son of Hanani
keyFigures.role: The seer who rebukes Jehoshaphat for helping Ahab.

keyFigures.name: Amariah
keyFigures.role: The chief priest, over all matters of the LORD.

keyFigures.name: Zebadiah
keyFigures.role: Ruler of the house of Judah, over all the king's matters.

keyThemes.explanation: Jehu rebukes Jehoshaphat but also names the good found in him.

keyThemes.theme: Justice in the fear of God
keyThemes.explanation: Judges are told they judge for the LORD, who takes no bribes.
Jehoshaphat tells the leaders to act faithfully and with courage.

2 Chronicles 20.summary: A great army of Moabites, Ammonites, and others comes against Judah, and Jehoshaphat proclaims a fast (2 Chronicles 20:1–4). Standing in the temple court, he prays, "neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee" (2 Chronicles 20:5–13). The Spirit of the LORD comes on Jahaziel, a Levite, who says, "the battle is not yours, but God's" (2 Chronicles 20:14–19). Jehoshaphat sets singers before the army, and as they praise, the LORD sets ambushes and the enemies destroy one another (2 Chronicles 20:20–25). Judah blesses the LORD in the valley of Berachah and returns to Jerusalem with joy (2 Chronicles 20:26–30). Jehoshaphat reigns twenty-five years, but his shipping venture with Ahaziah of Israel is wrecked, as the prophet Eliezer foretold (2 Chronicles 20:31–37).
2 Chronicles 20.whereWeAre: Jehoshaphat set up judges in chapter 19. Now a huge army invades, and Judah fasts and prays and is told "the battle is not yours, but God's" (2 Chronicles 20:15). Chapter 21 begins the evil reign of his son Jehoram.

keyFigures.name: Jehoshaphat
keyFigures.role: Proclaims a fast, prays, and puts singers before the army.

keyFigures.name: Jahaziel
keyFigures.role: A Levite on whom the Spirit comes, who says the battle is God's.

keyFigures.name: The Levite singers
keyFigures.role: Praise the LORD as Judah goes out to meet the enemy.

keyFigures.name: The invaders
keyFigures.role: Moab, Ammon, and mount Seir, who end up destroying one another.

keyFigures.name: Ahaziah
keyFigures.role: King of Israel, who joins Jehoshaphat in building ships.

keyFigures.name: Eliezer
keyFigures.role: A prophet who foretells that the ships will be broken.

keyThemes.explanation: Afraid, Jehoshaphat sets himself to seek the LORD and calls a fast.
The king admits Judah does not know what to do, but its eyes are on God.
Judah wins without fighting while the singers praise.
Judah names the valley Berachah because they blessed the LORD there.

2 Chronicles 21.summary: Jehoram becomes king and kills all his brothers (2 Chronicles 21:1–4). He walks in the ways of Ahab's house, yet the LORD will not destroy David's house because of his covenant (2 Chronicles 21:5–7). Edom and Libnah revolt, and Jehoram builds high places and leads Judah astray (2 Chronicles 21:8–11). A writing from Elijah warns of a great plague on his people and a disease of his bowels (2 Chronicles 21:12–15). The Philistines and Arabians carry off his goods, wives, and sons except the youngest, and after two years of sickness he dies "without being desired" (2 Chronicles 21:16–20).
2 Chronicles 21.whereWeAre: Jehoshaphat's reign ended in chapter 20 with a victory won by praise. His son Jehoram kills his brothers, follows Ahab's ways, and dies of a terrible disease after a warning from Elijah. In chapter 22 his son Ahaziah reigns only one year.

keyFigures.name: Jehoram
keyFigures.role: Kills his brothers, follows Ahab's ways, and dies of a painful disease.

keyFigures.name: The Edomites
keyFigures.role: Revolt and make their own king.

keyFigures.name: Elijah
keyFigures.role: Sends Jehoram a written warning of judgment.

keyFigures.name: The Philistines and Arabians
keyFigures.role: Raid Judah and carry off the king's family and goods.

keyThemes.explanation: Jehoram's marriage to Ahab's daughter leads him into Ahab's ways.

keyThemes.theme: God keeps his promise to David
keyThemes.explanation: Even under an evil king, God will not destroy David's line.
Elijah's letter warns Jehoram, and the disease he foretold comes.

2 Chronicles 22.summary: The people make Ahaziah, Jehoram's youngest son, king, and his mother Athaliah counsels him to do wickedly (2 Chronicles 22:1–4). He goes with Jehoram of Israel to war at Ramothgilead and later visits him at Jezreel (2 Chronicles 22:5–6). There Jehu, whom the LORD anointed to cut off Ahab's house, kills the princes of Judah and then Ahaziah (2 Chronicles 22:7–9). Athaliah destroys the royal family and takes the throne, but Jehoshabeath hides the baby Joash, and he stays hidden in the house of God six years (2 Chronicles 22:10–12).
2 Chronicles 22.whereWeAre: Jehoram died unmourned in chapter 21. Now his son Ahaziah is killed in Jehu's revolt, and Athaliah kills the royal family to take the throne, but the baby Joash is hidden in the temple. Chapter 23 tells how he is crowned.

keyFigures.name: Ahaziah
keyFigures.role: Jehoram's son, who follows his mother's counsel and is killed by Jehu.

keyFigures.name: Athaliah
keyFigures.role: Ahaziah's mother, who destroys the royal family and seizes the throne.

keyFigures.name: Jehu
keyFigures.role: Anointed by the LORD to cut off Ahab's house; he kills Ahaziah.

keyFigures.name: Jehoshabeath
keyFigures.role: The king's daughter and Jehoiada's wife, who hides the baby Joash.

keyFigures.name: Joash
keyFigures.role: The infant prince, hidden in the temple for six years.

keyThemes.explanation: Ahaziah follows his mother and Ahab's house "to his destruction."
Ahaziah dies in God's judgment on the house of Ahab.
One baby, hidden by a brave woman, keeps David's line alive.

2 Chronicles 23.summary: In the seventh year Jehoiada the priest makes a covenant with the captains and Levites, and they agree to make Joash king (2 Chronicles 23:1–3). Jehoiada places Levites and people to guard the temple and arms the captains with David's spears and shields (2 Chronicles 23:4–10). They crown Joash, give him the testimony, and anoint him, shouting, "God save the king" (2 Chronicles 23:11). Athaliah cries "Treason, Treason," and she is taken out and killed at the horse gate (2 Chronicles 23:12–15). Jehoiada makes a covenant that the people will be the LORD's, they tear down the house of Baal, and Joash is set on the throne (2 Chronicles 23:16–21).
2 Chronicles 23.whereWeAre: The infant Joash was hidden in the temple for six years in chapter 22. Now Jehoiada the priest brings him out and crowns him, and Athaliah is put to death. In chapter 24 Joash repairs the temple.

keyFigures.name: Jehoiada
keyFigures.role: The priest who crowns Joash and leads the covenant.

keyFigures.name: Joash
keyFigures.role: Crowned king at seven.

keyFigures.name: Athaliah
keyFigures.role: Cries "Treason" and is put to death.

keyFigures.name: The captains and Levites
keyFigures.role: Guard the temple and the young king.

keyFigures.name: The people of the land
keyFigures.role: Rejoice, tear down Baal's house, and kill his priest Mattan.

keyThemes.explanation: Jehoiada sets the son of David back on the throne.
Jehoiada leads the king and people in a covenant to be the LORD's people.
Baal's house is torn down, and temple service is set in order again.

2 Chronicles 24.summary: Joash becomes king at seven and does right "all the days of Jehoiada the priest" (2 Chronicles 24:1–3). He has a chest set at the temple gate, the people gladly fill it, and the house of God is repaired (2 Chronicles 24:4–14). Jehoiada dies at 130 and is buried among the kings because he had done good in Israel (2 Chronicles 24:15–16). Then the princes lead Joash to serve idols, and when Zechariah son of Jehoiada rebukes them, Joash has him stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:17–22). A small Syrian army defeats Judah, and Joash's servants kill him in his bed (2 Chronicles 24:23–27).
2 Chronicles 24.whereWeAre: Joash was crowned at seven in chapter 23. He repairs the temple while Jehoiada lives, but after Jehoiada dies he turns to idols and has the priest's son stoned. In chapter 25 his son Amaziah becomes king.

keyFigures.name: Joash
keyFigures.role: Repairs the temple, then turns to idols and has Zechariah stoned.

keyFigures.name: Jehoiada
keyFigures.role: The priest who guides Joash and is buried among the kings.

keyFigures.name: The princes of Judah
keyFigures.role: Lead Joash to serve idols after Jehoiada dies.

keyFigures.name: Zechariah son of Jehoiada
keyFigures.role: Rebukes the people and is stoned in the temple court.

keyFigures.name: The Syrians
keyFigures.role: Defeat Judah's larger army with a small company.

keyFigures.name: Zabad and Jehozabad
keyFigures.role: Joash's servants, who kill him in his bed.

keyThemes.explanation: The people gladly fill the chest to repair the house of God.
Joash does right only while Jehoiada lives.
Joash stones the son of the man who saved his life.
Judah loses to a small Syrian army because it forsook the LORD.

2 Chronicles 25.summary: Amaziah does right, "but not with a perfect heart," and he kills his father's murderers but spares their children, as the law of Moses commands (2 Chronicles 25:1–4). He hires 100,000 soldiers from Israel, but a man of God warns him, and he sends them home (2 Chronicles 25:5–10). Amaziah defeats Edom in the valley of salt, while the soldiers he sent away raid the cities of Judah (2 Chronicles 25:11–13). He then sets up the gods of Edom and silences the prophet who rebukes him (2 Chronicles 25:14–16). He challenges Joash king of Israel, who defeats him, breaks down Jerusalem's wall, and takes the temple's gold (2 Chronicles 25:17–24). Later a conspiracy forms against Amaziah, and he is killed at Lachish (2 Chronicles 25:25–28).
2 Chronicles 25.whereWeAre: Joash was killed by his own servants in chapter 24. His son Amaziah defeats Edom, then worships Edom's gods and is beaten by Joash king of Israel. In chapter 26 his son Uzziah has a long reign.

keyFigures.name: Amaziah
keyFigures.role: Defeats Edom, then worships its gods and is defeated by Israel.

keyFigures.name: A man of God
keyFigures.role: Warns Amaziah not to take Israel's soldiers to war.

keyFigures.name: A prophet
keyFigures.role: Asks why Amaziah seeks gods that could not save their own people.

keyFigures.name: Joash king of Israel
keyFigures.role: Answers with a parable, then defeats Amaziah and breaks Jerusalem's wall.

keyThemes.explanation: Amaziah does right, but not with a perfect heart.
The man of God tells Amaziah the LORD can repay what he loses by obeying.
After victory Amaziah turns to Edom's gods and picks a fight he cannot win.

2 Chronicles 26.summary: Uzziah becomes king at sixteen and reigns fifty-two years, and while he seeks God, God makes him prosper (2 Chronicles 26:1–5). He defeats the Philistines and Arabians, builds towers, digs wells, and loves farming (2 Chronicles 26:6–10). He builds a large army and sets on Jerusalem's towers machines that shoot arrows and great stones (2 Chronicles 26:11–15). But "when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction," and he goes into the temple to burn incense (2 Chronicles 26:16). Azariah and eighty priests stand against him, and leprosy breaks out on his forehead while he rages (2 Chronicles 26:17–20). He lives apart as a leper until he dies, while his son Jotham rules (2 Chronicles 26:21–23).
2 Chronicles 26.whereWeAre: Amaziah was killed in a conspiracy in chapter 25. His son Uzziah grows strong while he seeks God, but pride leads him to burn incense in the temple, and he becomes a leper. Chapter 27 tells of his son Jotham.

keyFigures.name: Uzziah
keyFigures.role: Prospers while he seeks God, then is struck with leprosy for burning incense.

keyFigures.name: Zechariah
keyFigures.role: Has "understanding in the visions of God" and guides Uzziah.

keyFigures.name: Azariah the priest
keyFigures.role: Leads eighty priests to stop the king in the temple.

keyFigures.name: Jotham
keyFigures.role: Uzziah's son, who rules the people while his father lives apart.

keyThemes.explanation: As long as Uzziah seeks the LORD, God makes him prosper.
When Uzziah becomes strong, his heart is lifted up to his destruction.
Burning incense belongs to the priests, and even the king may not take it.

2 Chronicles 27.summary: Jotham becomes king and does right, though the people still act corruptly (2 Chronicles 27:1–2). He builds the high gate of the temple, cities, and towers, and he makes the Ammonites pay tribute for three years (2 Chronicles 27:3–5). Jotham becomes mighty "because he prepared his ways before the LORD his God" (2 Chronicles 27:6). He dies after sixteen years, and his son Ahaz becomes king (2 Chronicles 27:7–9).
2 Chronicles 27.whereWeAre: Uzziah died a leper in chapter 26. His son Jotham follows the LORD and grows mighty, though the people still act corruptly. In chapter 28 his son Ahaz leads Judah into deep idolatry.

keyFigures.name: Jotham
keyFigures.role: Does right, builds, defeats the Ammonites, and becomes mighty.

keyFigures.name: The Ammonites
keyFigures.role: Pay Jotham tribute for three years.

keyThemes.explanation: Jotham becomes mighty because he prepared his ways before the LORD.

keyThemes.theme: A good king, a corrupt people
keyThemes.explanation: The king does right while the people still act corruptly.
Jotham builds the temple's high gate and cities and castles in the hills and forests.

2 Chronicles 28.summary: Ahaz makes images for Baalim and burns his children in the fire (2 Chronicles 28:1–4). God gives him into the hands of Syria and of Pekah king of Israel, who kills 120,000 men of Judah in one day and takes 200,000 captives (2 Chronicles 28:5–8). The prophet Oded warns Israel's army to send the captives back, and leaders of Ephraim clothe, feed, and return them to Jericho (2 Chronicles 28:9–15). Ahaz asks the king of Assyria for help, but Tilgathpilneser only distresses him (2 Chronicles 28:16–21). In his distress Ahaz sins even more, sacrificing to the gods of Damascus and shutting the doors of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 28:22–25). He dies and is not buried in the tombs of the kings (2 Chronicles 28:26–27).
2 Chronicles 28.whereWeAre: Jotham's short, faithful reign ended in chapter 27. Now Ahaz worships Baal, loses battles to Syria and Israel, and shuts the temple doors. In chapter 29 his son Hezekiah opens them again.

keyFigures.name: Ahaz
keyFigures.role: Worships Baalim, shuts the temple doors, and seeks help from Assyria.

keyFigures.name: Pekah
keyFigures.role: King of Israel, who kills 120,000 men of Judah in one day.

keyFigures.name: Oded
keyFigures.role: A prophet who tells Israel's army to send the captives home.

keyFigures.name: The heads of Ephraim
keyFigures.role: Clothe, feed, and return the captives to Jericho.

keyFigures.name: Tilgathpilneser
keyFigures.role: King of Assyria, who distresses Ahaz instead of helping him.

keyThemes.explanation: Ahaz's idols bring defeat by Syria, Israel, Edom, and the Philistines.
Israel's leaders listen to the prophet and care for their captives from Judah.
Instead of turning to God in distress, Ahaz sins even more.

2 Chronicles 29.summary: In the first month of his reign, Hezekiah opens and repairs the doors of the temple (2 Chronicles 29:1–3). He tells the priests and Levites to sanctify themselves and the house, because their fathers' sins brought God's wrath (2 Chronicles 29:4–11). The Levites cleanse the house in sixteen days and carry the filth out to the brook Kidron (2 Chronicles 29:12–19). Hezekiah offers sin offerings for all Israel, and as the burnt offering begins, the Levites play David's instruments and the singers praise (2 Chronicles 29:20–30). The people bring so many offerings that the Levites help the priests, and all rejoice, "for the thing was done suddenly" (2 Chronicles 29:31–36).
2 Chronicles 29.whereWeAre: Ahaz shut the temple doors in chapter 28. In the first month of his reign, Hezekiah opens them, has the temple cleansed, and restores its sacrifices and songs. Chapter 30 calls all Israel to keep the Passover.

keyFigures.name: Hezekiah
keyFigures.role: Opens the temple doors and restores its worship.

keyFigures.name: The Levites
keyFigures.role: Sanctify themselves, cleanse the house, and lead the songs.

keyFigures.name: The priests
keyFigures.role: Offer the sin offerings and burnt offerings for all Israel.

keyFigures.name: The congregation
keyFigures.role: Worship and bring offerings beyond what the priests can prepare.

keyThemes.explanation: Hezekiah opens the doors his father shut and cleanses the house.
Hezekiah admits the sins of their fathers and seeks a covenant with God.
Songs, trumpets, and offerings fill the restored temple.

2 Chronicles 30.summary: Hezekiah and the people decide to keep the Passover in the second month, since the priests were not ready in the first (2 Chronicles 30:1–5). Runners carry letters from Beersheba to Dan, calling Israel to return to the LORD, for he "is gracious and merciful" (2 Chronicles 30:6–9). Many in the north laugh at them, but some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humble themselves and come (2 Chronicles 30:10–12). A great crowd removes the altars in Jerusalem and keeps the Passover, and Hezekiah prays for those who eat it without being cleansed, and the LORD heals the people (2 Chronicles 30:13–20). They keep the feast seven days and then seven more, with joy not seen since Solomon (2 Chronicles 30:21–27).
2 Chronicles 30.whereWeAre: Hezekiah restored the temple's worship in chapter 29. Now he invites Judah and what is left of the northern tribes to a great Passover in Jerusalem. In chapter 31 the people tear down idols and bring their tithes.

keyFigures.name: Hezekiah
keyFigures.role: Invites all Israel to the Passover and prays for the unclean.

keyFigures.name: The posts
keyFigures.role: Runners who carry the king's letters from city to city.

keyFigures.name: The remnant of Israel
keyFigures.role: Some mock, but some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun come.

keyFigures.name: The priests and Levites
keyFigures.role: Kill the Passover lambs and bless the people.

keyThemes.explanation: Hezekiah invites even the northern tribes to come back to the LORD.
The letters promise that God is gracious and will not turn his face away.
Hezekiah prays for people who seek God but are not cleansed, and God heals them.
The feast is doubled, and Jerusalem has joy not seen since Solomon.

2 Chronicles 31.summary: After the Passover the people go out and break down the images, groves, and high places across the land (2 Chronicles 31:1). Hezekiah sets the priests and Levites in their courses and commands the people to give the priests' portion (2 Chronicles 31:2–4). The people bring firstfruits and tithes in heaps from the third month to the seventh (2 Chronicles 31:5–10). Hezekiah prepares storerooms and appoints Cononiah, Shimei, and others to oversee and share out the gifts (2 Chronicles 31:11–19). In every work he began, Hezekiah "did it with all his heart, and prospered" (2 Chronicles 31:20–21).
2 Chronicles 31.whereWeAre: The great Passover ended in joy in chapter 30. Now the people destroy idols across the land and bring so many gifts that they lie in heaps. In chapter 32 Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah.

keyFigures.name: Hezekiah
keyFigures.role: Sets the priests and Levites in order and has storerooms built.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Bring firstfruits and tithes in heaps.

keyFigures.name: Azariah
keyFigures.role: The chief priest, who reports that there is plenty left over.

keyFigures.name: Cononiah and Shimei
keyFigures.role: Levites put in charge of the gifts.

keyFigures.name: Kore
keyFigures.role: Over the freewill offerings.

keyThemes.explanation: The people go home and destroy the idols in the land.
The people give so much that the gifts lie in heaps.
Hezekiah does every work with all his heart and prospers.

2 Chronicles 32.summary: Sennacherib king of Assyria invades Judah, and Hezekiah stops the springs outside the city and builds up the walls (2 Chronicles 32:1–5). He tells the people, "With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God to help us" (2 Chronicles 32:6–8). Sennacherib's servants mock Hezekiah and the LORD in speeches and letters (2 Chronicles 32:9–19). Hezekiah and Isaiah pray, and the LORD sends an angel who cuts off the Assyrian army, and Sennacherib is killed by his own sons (2 Chronicles 32:20–23). Hezekiah becomes sick and is healed, but his heart is lifted up until he humbles himself (2 Chronicles 32:24–26). He grows very rich, brings Gihon's water to the west side of the city, and dies honored by all Judah (2 Chronicles 32:27–33).
2 Chronicles 32.whereWeAre: Hezekiah reorganized worship in chapter 31. Now Assyria invades, Hezekiah prays, and an angel destroys the Assyrian army; later his heart is lifted up in pride. In chapter 33 his son Manasseh undoes his reforms.

keyFigures.name: Hezekiah
keyFigures.role: Prepares Jerusalem, prays, and is healed, but grows proud.

keyFigures.name: Sennacherib
keyFigures.role: King of Assyria, who invades and mocks the LORD.

keyFigures.name: Isaiah
keyFigures.role: The prophet who prays with Hezekiah.

keyFigures.name: Sennacherib's servants
keyFigures.role: Taunt the people of Jerusalem in their own language.

keyFigures.name: The angel of the LORD
keyFigures.role: Cuts off the leaders of the Assyrian camp.

keyFigures.name: The princes of Babylon
keyFigures.role: Send ambassadors to ask about the wonder in the land.

keyThemes.explanation: Hezekiah tells the people that more are with them than with Assyria.
Assyria mocks the LORD as one of the idols, and God destroys its army.
Hezekiah's heart is lifted up, and God leaves him to test what is in his heart.

2 Chronicles 33.summary: Manasseh becomes king at twelve and rebuilds the high places, sets altars for Baalim and the stars in the temple courts, and burns his children in the fire (2 Chronicles 33:1–9). The LORD speaks to him and the people, but they will not listen (2 Chronicles 33:10). The captains of Assyria bind Manasseh and carry him to Babylon, where he humbles himself and prays, and God brings him back to Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 33:11–13). He removes the foreign gods, repairs the LORD's altar, and commands Judah to serve the LORD (2 Chronicles 33:14–20). His son Amon does evil and never humbles himself, and his servants kill him after two years (2 Chronicles 33:21–25).
2 Chronicles 33.whereWeAre: Hezekiah died honored at the end of chapter 32. His son Manasseh leads Judah to do worse than the heathen but repents in chains in Babylon, while his son Amon never humbles himself. In chapter 34 young Josiah takes the throne.

keyFigures.name: Manasseh
keyFigures.role: Leads Judah into great evil, then repents in Babylon and is restored.

keyFigures.name: The captains of Assyria
keyFigures.role: Bind Manasseh and carry him to Babylon.

keyFigures.name: Amon
keyFigures.role: Does evil, never humbles himself, and is killed by his servants.

keyFigures.name: The people of the land
keyFigures.role: Kill Amon's murderers and make Josiah king.

keyThemes.explanation: Even Manasseh, who led Judah into great evil, is restored when he humbles himself.
After returning, Manasseh removes idols and commands Judah to serve the LORD.
Amon follows his father's sins but not his repentance.

2 Chronicles 34.summary: Josiah becomes king at eight, begins to seek God at sixteen, and at twenty begins to purge Judah and Jerusalem of idols (2 Chronicles 34:1–3). He breaks down the altars of Baalim and burns the bones of their priests, even in the cities of the northern tribes (2 Chronicles 34:4–7). In his eighteenth year he repairs the temple, and Hilkiah the priest finds "a book of the law of the LORD given by Moses" (2 Chronicles 34:8–14). Shaphan reads it to the king, and Josiah tears his clothes and sends to the prophetess Huldah (2 Chronicles 34:15–22). Huldah says the curses in the book will come, but not in Josiah's days, because his heart was tender (2 Chronicles 34:23–28). Josiah reads the book to the people, makes a covenant before the LORD, and leads them to serve God all his days (2 Chronicles 34:29–33).
2 Chronicles 34.whereWeAre: Amon was killed by his servants in chapter 33. Young Josiah seeks God, purges idols, and leads the people in covenant after the book of the law is found in the temple. In chapter 35 he keeps a great Passover.

keyFigures.name: Josiah
keyFigures.role: Seeks God, purges idols, and makes a covenant before the LORD.

keyFigures.name: Hilkiah
keyFigures.role: The high priest who finds the book of the law in the temple.

keyFigures.name: Shaphan
keyFigures.role: The scribe who reads the book to the king.

keyFigures.name: Huldah
keyFigures.role: The prophetess who tells what will happen to Jerusalem and to Josiah.

keyThemes.explanation: Josiah begins to seek God while he is still young.
When the law is read, Josiah tears his clothes and seeks the LORD.
God delays judgment because Josiah humbled himself.
Josiah leads the people to promise to keep God's commands with all their heart.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: The discovery of the book of the law and Huldah's response.

2 Chronicles 35.summary: Josiah keeps the Passover in the first month and sets the priests and Levites in their places (2 Chronicles 35:1–6). He gives 30,000 lambs and kids and 3,000 bullocks from his own flocks, and his princes give freely too (2 Chronicles 35:7–9). The priests, Levites, singers, and porters serve in order, and no Passover like it had been kept since Samuel (2 Chronicles 35:10–19). Necho king of Egypt warns Josiah that God sent him, but Josiah disguises himself and fights at Megiddo (2 Chronicles 35:20–22). Archers wound Josiah, and he dies in Jerusalem, mourned by all Judah and by Jeremiah (2 Chronicles 35:23–27).
2 Chronicles 35.whereWeAre: Josiah renewed the covenant in chapter 34. Now he keeps a Passover unlike any since Samuel, then dies in battle against Necho of Egypt. Chapter 36 tells of Judah's last kings and the fall of Jerusalem.

keyFigures.name: Josiah
keyFigures.role: Keeps a great Passover and dies in battle at Megiddo.

keyFigures.name: The priests and Levites
keyFigures.role: Prepare and serve the Passover as the law commands.

keyFigures.name: Necho
keyFigures.role: King of Egypt, who warns Josiah not to fight him.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Laments for Josiah.

keyThemes.explanation: The Passover is kept as the law of Moses and David's plan direct.
The king and his princes give animals for the people's offerings.
Josiah ignores the warning from God through Necho and dies.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Josiah's Passover celebration, with different amounts of detail.

2 Chronicles 36.summary: The king of Egypt removes Jehoahaz after three months and sets up Jehoiakim, who is later bound by Nebuchadnezzar (2 Chronicles 36:1–8). Jehoiachin reigns three months and is taken to Babylon, and Zedekiah reigns eleven years and will not humble himself before Jeremiah (2 Chronicles 36:9–13). The priests and people pollute the temple and mock God's messengers "till there was no remedy" (2 Chronicles 36:14–16). The king of the Chaldees kills young and old, burns the house of God, breaks down Jerusalem's walls, and carries the survivors to Babylon (2 Chronicles 36:17–21). In his first year Cyrus king of Persia proclaims that the LORD has charged him to build a house in Jerusalem and invites God's people to "go up" (2 Chronicles 36:22–23).
2 Chronicles 36.whereWeAre: Josiah died at Megiddo in chapter 35. Four kings follow, the people mock God's messengers, and Babylon burns the temple. The book ends with Cyrus of Persia letting the exiles go home, and Ezra 1 begins with the same decree.

keyFigures.name: Jehoiakim
keyFigures.role: Set up as king by Egypt and later bound by Nebuchadnezzar.

keyFigures.name: Zedekiah
keyFigures.role: Judah's last king, who will not humble himself and rebels.

keyFigures.name: Nebuchadnezzar
keyFigures.role: King of Babylon, who destroys Jerusalem and the temple.

keyFigures.name: Cyrus
keyFigures.role: King of Persia, whose decree lets God's people go up to Jerusalem.

keyThemes.explanation: God keeps sending messengers because he has compassion on his people.
When they keep mocking his prophets, God's wrath comes until there is no remedy.
The exile and the return both fulfill what God spoke through Jeremiah.
The book ends with an invitation to go up and rebuild God's house.
